mentions.text: We are really terrible at predicting what's easy and what's hard -- 15 years ago we were screaming at truck drivers to learn to code, lol. Another really fun story I like -- what if in the summer of 2020 (GPT-3 release) someone told you that language model was about as close to self-driving as Tesla's Autopilot was, with it's billions of miles of data and vision-first approach. Would have sounded nutty, but VLAs drive cars now. My lack of surprisal is mostly appreciating the uncertainty in dealing with unknowns. But I generally agree, there's a lot of takes now about "RH fell, cancer is next", and I'm very skeptical. We'll probably see lots of progress in parts of biology or physics that already have ready-made verification systems, there's probably lots of business opportunities in building physical verifiers, and there's probably a lot potential in applying existing methods to larger data sets like the Vera Rubin telescope. But what if you need a 50B telescope and 20 years to build it in order to verify some physics hypothesis? What if you do need a RCT across a population to verify a new drug hypothesis? Progress will look a lot like classical progress then, despite AI.

mentions.text: Net income at IPO, time to first profitable quarter. Caveat that there's a lot of creative accounting in tech, and it's gotten more creative with AI companies. Amazon (1997): -$5.78 million - first profitable quarter Q4 '01 Netflix (2002): -$21 million - first profitable quarter Q2 '03 Tesla (2010): -$154 million - first profitable quarter Q1 '13 Facebook (2012): +$1 billion at IPO Anthropic (2026): -$100 billion through sept 2026 One of these things is not like the other. Anthropic's financials on serving existing models are great , their debt to stay relevant going forward is atrocious, and their competitive moat depends entirely on continuing (and accelerating) that spending. Amazon, netflix, tesla, and facebook did not need to spend exponentially more money to become profitable.

mentions.text: Where subscriptions make sense: On my Tesla I occasionally pay to get the FSD for a month e.g. summer road trips and then turn it off. I understand the hw is already there but I also understand I am paying for the FSD software (per use) and not just the hw. Where they do not: The other car in our family, a 2015 Acura has outdated maps. It often takes to a street that is either now a one-way or completely cut off. It also misses shorter new roads. To update the maps, Acura will charge me $500!! In the meanwhile, my HP printer promises 1000 pages for a XL cartridge but runs out of ink 200 pages (text only, no images). I've already spent 20x of the printer cost on the cartridges. I sure wish there was a law against this.
